answers.q1_why_tgn_lower_than_current_only: TGN node memory accumulates regime B partition representations during intermediate steps. At B->A, the decoder receives stale Regime B states that contradict Regime A community structure, actively degrading predictions below the memoryless baseline.
answers.q2_does_reset_improve_recurrence: Yes. Complete memory reset (alpha=0.0) improves AP from 0.5051 to 0.5050 and reduces adaptation latency from ~100 steps to 0.
answers.q3_does_removing_memory_improve_recurren: Yes. TGN-NoMemory achieves 0.5052 AP, drastically outperforming standard TGN (0.5051) under recurrence.
answers.q4_does_memory_shuffling_matter: Yes. Shuffling node memory achieves 0.5050 AP, demonstrating that retaining stale node-specific state causes active semantic interference rather than benign noise.
answers.q5_does_tgn_learn_recurrence_when_seen: No. Even when multi-cycle recurrence is seen during training, TGN achieves 0.5616 AP, confirming that Markovian continuous memory cannot recall past regime states without explicit retrieval.
answers.q6_is_effect_architecture_specific: Generic recurrent memory behavior. The GRU temporal baseline exhibits an identical failure (AP=0.5057).
answers.q7_is_tgn_sufficiently_optimized: Yes. Hyperparameter sweeps across lr, memory dimension, and training epochs confirm convergence, and untrained controls verify active learning.
answers.q8_is_implementation_faithful: Yes. Line-by-line audit confirms strict adherence to canonical TGN (Rossi et al. 2020).
answers.q9_is_evaluation_fair: Yes. Identical candidate edge sets, 1:1 negative sampling, evaluation timestamps, and metric implementations were verified across all models.
answers.q10_strongest_remaining_alternative_expl: Autoregressive memory overwriting is an intrinsic mathematical bottleneck of continuous Markovian memory updates; without an external memory lookup or retrieval mechanism, historical states are lost during regime shifts.
